title: Caruana, Niemann Sweep Praggnanandhaa, Vaishali; Assaubayeva Upsets Arjun
summary:
GMs Fabiano Caruana and Hans Niemann are the two players to score six points (or two wins) on day three of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026. Caruana leads Group B with 10 points and a 3077 performance after sweeping GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu. Niemann won both games against GM Vaishali Rameshbabu to co-lead Group D with GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave with eight points apiece.

GM Alireza Firouzja leads Group A with eight points, while GMs Ian Nepomniachtchi and Haik Martirosyan co-lead Group C with six points. In Group D as well, GM Bibisara Assaubayeva won the Game of the Day with her career-best upset against GM Arjun Erigaisi, even if she lost the second game.

Day four, which features rounds five and six of the Group Stage, is on Friday, November 13, starting at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30 p.m. IST.

Group A: Firouzja Leads As Duda Falters

Group B: Caruana Leads, Le Comes Close

Group C: Martirosyan, Giri Trade Punches; Carlsen Survives Vs. Mishra

Group D: Niemann Sweeps Vaishali, So Gives Up Vs. Vachier-Lagrave

The fast classic time control set the stage for plenty of drama. The majority of games were decisive, with eight wins coming in the day's first round and five in the day's second. We saw a few miniatures and one major upset, but also several missed opportunities. It was also a happy birthday for IM Anna Rudolf, who conducted pre- and post-game interviews on the ground.

The birthday girl. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Keep reading, but you may also be interested in watching GM Hikaru Nakamura's video recap, embedded below.

Group A: Firouzja Leads As Duda Falters

Firouzja and GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda started the day sharing the lead on four points. Firouzja beat GM Jorden van Foreest and then drew, while Duda won game one and lost game two against GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov to fall a point behind.

Group A Standings

Van Foreest put up great defense in game one, even if he lost it. Although he was outplayed in the middlegame where he lost two pawns, he pulled a great escape by trading queens into a holdable endgame, a miracle. But with both players under a minute, the pendulum swung back the other way as Van Foreest didn't find 62...Kd4!, which virtually by force wins back the b3-pawn, and the French number-one scored his three points after all.

Van Foreest got his chances with White in the next game, against the French number-one's French Defense, but Firouzja survived the attack to hold onto the lead.

Firouzja won the mini-match against Van Foreest. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Duda stayed on course in the first game after winning an outrageously complicated and long 92-move game against Abdusattorov. But the Uzbek star struck in game two with the black pieces, even if there was a narrow way for Duda to survive in the endgame (both games ended in knight endgames).

Abdusattorov vs. Duda ended 3-3. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

The biggest regret for the Polish grandmaster may be missing the winning sacrifice 17.Bxh6!, a move that GM David Howell said fit his attacking style. The "quiet" followup of 18.Bh3! was perhaps what made the combination difficult to find, as Duda had almost 19 minutes, and took three minutes to play the game move.

A loss in that game could have spelled disaster for Abdusattorov, who is already set to lose six rating points with two losses—after finishing 22nd in the Blitz Tiebreaker. As for Duda, he is still just one point off from the lead.

Remember that Bxh6 motif, by the way, as Caruana had a similar sacrifice in his game, which he played!

Caruana and Rapport before the game. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Group B: Caruana Leads, Le Comes Close

Caruana was the star of the show in Group B as he won both games against the formidable Praggnanandhaa, who finds himself in last place.

Group B Standings

"Of course, today couldn't have gone better," said Caruana, who "really wasn't even playing for a win" in game two but capitalized when he got the chance in the endgame.

Game one was a 26-move miniature, and Caruana said he spotted the idea when he played 17.b3. He said, "I was looking at this sacrifice, because he wants to stop some Ng5 ideas, so it makes sense to at least consider it. And I didn't expect he would play it because it looked very dangerous for him. I didn't hesitate too much."

I didn't hesitate too much.

—Fabiano Caruana

Praggnanandhaa collapsed in a slightly worse endgame in the second game. Although he's eight points behind the leader, he showed in Norway Chess 2026—which he won with four consecutive wins—that it's almost never too late for a comeback, especially as each win is worth three points.

GM Liem Le, two points behind Caruana, nearly won his two games against GM Vincent Keymer, but didn't manage to put away the second one. Le won a rook endgame in game one, but game two featured an endgame miracle as promoting a second queen was the mistake.

Liem Le came close to matching Caruana's 10 points. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Group C: Martirosyan, Giri Trade Punches; Carlsen Survives Vs. Mishra

Nepomniachtchi stayed in the lead with two draws against GM Shakhriyar Mamedyarov (two points for the day), while Martirosyan caught up with one win and one loss against GM Anish Giri (three points). After GM Magnus Carlsen drew GM Abhimanyu Mishra in game one, he survived a lost position in game two and is still winless.

Group C Standings

On both days of the Group Stage, Martirosyan has recovered from a loss by winning in game two. His lead comes to show that here, unlike in regular classical tournaments, a win and a loss is better than two draws. He said, "It's not my plan obviously, but it's working very well! (...) I got my chance with Black and I took it."

Martirosyan, so far the master of comebacks. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Against Martirosyan, Giri won game one convincingly with a 26-move miniature, the same number of moves as Caruana's first win. He explained, "He got a bad version of some theoretical variation... I think I had a very strong attack, and at the very least I always thought I had great attacking play," and at most it was a forced win.

Giri also had the shortest confessional visit so far, lasting about five or six seconds. He came just before the conclusion of the game to say, "I think it's checkmate."

Anish Giri enters the confessional booth for about six seconds! "I think it's checkmate." https://t.co/4HK5ckn01d https://t.co/AA3AmtcUaG

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 12, 2026

In game two, however, things backfired, and Giri candidly admitted, with a smile, "I am super pissed, to be honest." It ended with a crazy time scramble where Martirosyan said it's easier to play with White given the time control.

Nepomniachtchi, after two theoretically interesting but accurate draws with Mamedyarov, remains in the lead. In the interview, he said he was disappointed. But we can surely say that there are two players, at the bottom of the standings, who hoped for a different outcome on day three.

A memorable match for Mishra, but not for the best reason. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

After holding a solid draw in game one, Mishra outplayed the world number-one with the white pieces against the Scandinavian Defense. Carlsen was worse for some time, managed to trade queens, and blundered in the endgame. Down two pawns, he ultimately held from the following position by trading into an opposite-color bishop endgame.

"In some ways it went well, but of course you really should win such a game," said Mishra after the game. He saw the bright side, too, however: "I'll take that I played on par with Magnus. I get this new confidence that absolutely anyone in the world I can match, but still, not winning hurts a lot."

You really should win such a game.

—Abhimanyu Mishra

Both players have reason to be disappointed. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Carlsen has made four draws and will look to win his first on Friday. Although he's played Martirosyan in rapid and blitz, it will be their first classical encounter.

Group D: Niemann Sweeps Vaishali, So Gives Up Vs. Vachier-Lagrave

Vachier-Lagrave picked up one win and a draw against GM Wesley So, while Niemann won both games against Vaishali to catch up to the lead. Assaubayeva scored her biggest upset against Arjun.

Group D Standings

We can start with the upset, which Assaubayeva assessed as her best game this year. She said, "I am just happy that I won because before the tournament I was scared to score zero out of everything." Like World Championship Challenger Javokhir Sindarov, she isn't afraid to play the King's Indian Defense with the black pieces at an elite tournament.

Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Before beating the 2746-rated Arjun, Assaubayeva's highest-rated upset was against 2691-rated GM Sanan Sjugirov. GM Rafael Leitao goes over that fight below.

Arjun won the second game to land three points (or one win) behind the leaders.

Like the day before, Vachier-Lagrave won the first game and drew the second. In the first game, he managed to break So's Berlin Defense when the second player landed in a position with tripled pawns. So actually had a chance to hold the queen endgame, but didn't find 56...Qe1+, the last chance.

With the white pieces in the second game, So made a quick draw with Vachier-Lagrave, following a theoretical draw in the Grunfeld Defense and ending the game with nearly seven more minutes than he started with.

Vachier-Lagrave with the white pieces. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

So said that he should avoid the fast classic time control from now on. He may change his mind, but asked whether he'll come back next year with a second, he repeated that he should stay away. He also said he was "not ready to keep up with five mini-matches."

"I think it's pretty clear I found my worst chess format... It's clear I have to stay away from this time control." -Wesley So after making an instant draw with MVL https://t.co/7yVTH0g3Bh

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 12, 2026

Niemann had a score to settle with Vaishali, who beat him in round one of the Blitz Tiebreaker. He said, "Everyone saw my first-round loss and they assumed I'm not a good blitz player anymore. They didn't see how I finished, in not the worst fashion. Anyway, we live in a short-form society, so that's okay." It was the only game he lost and he finished in fifth place with 5.5/9.

We live in a short-form society.

—Hans Niemann

Niemann bounced back from the blitz. Photo: Tor Nilssen/Total Chess.

The first player to win two games in one day, Niemann surmised, "In this time control, you really have to manage your time well, and I was able to keep up with the pressure and eventually she collapsed." In game two, he found a precise way to force his a-pawn through to promotion, showing just how bad a knight is at fighting against a rook pawn.

On the live rating list, Niemann is back over 2700.

Everything can still change as the players have played just four of 10 games in the Group Stage, with three points awarded per win. Check out the pairings for Friday for all four groups below.

Round 5 Pairings

How to watch?

You can review the event on the Chess24 Twitch or YouTube pages, or on GM Hikaru Nakamura's Kick channel. You can find the games on our dedicated events page.

The live broadcast was hosted by GM David Howell, IMs Jovanka Houska and Anna Rudolf, and WIM Fiona Steil-Antoni.

The Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 takes place on November 10-21 at the Anantara New York Palace Hotel in Budapest, Hungary. The event is a trial run for the official event in 2027, which will crown the first FIDE World Combined Champion. The event consists of a round-robin group stage and a knockout combining blitz, rapid, and fast classical time controls. additionalSources.title: Total Chess: Double wins for Caruana and Niemann, first 2700+ scalp for Assaubayeva
additionalSources.summary:
Fabiano Caruana and Hans Niemann scored back-to-back wins on Thursday at the Total Chess Pilot in Budapest, defeating Praggnanandhaa and Vaishali Rameshbabu respectively. Caruana now leads Group B with 10 points, while Niemann shares first place in Group D with Maxime Vachier-Lagrave. Meanwhile, Magnus Carlsen remains winless but just 2 points off the lead in Group C after again signing two draws. Notably, Bibisara Assaubayeva obtained a memorable upset victory over Arjun Erigaisi. | Photo: Michal Walusza / Total Chess

Carlsen escapes with a draw against Mishra

The second day of the group stage at the Total Chess Pilot in Budapest saw two players score maximum points, as Fabiano Caruana and Hans Niemann defeated their respective opponents twice on Thursday. Coincidentally, both Americans faced one of the Rameshbabu siblings, with Caruana beating Praggnanandhaa and Niemann defeating Vaishali. Caruana is now the highest scorer among all 24 participants, having collected 10 points from three wins and a draw under the football-style scoring system.

Caruana leads Group B outright, while Niemann shares first place in Group D with Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, both on 8 points. In Group A, Alireza Firouzja is the sole leader after collecting a win and a draw for the second consecutive day, also reaching 8 points.

Hans Niemann defeated Vaishali Rameshbabu twice (after the Indian GM had defeated him in the blitz tournament) and is now co-leader in Group D | Photo: Michal Walusza

Alireza Firouzja is leading Group A with 8 points | Photo: Michal Walusza

Meanwhile, Group C has the tightest standings, with Ian Nepomniachtchi and Haik Martirosyan sharing the lead on 6 points. The two have reached that score in contrasting fashion: Nepo defeated Abhimanyu Mishra once and drew his other three games, while Martirosyan has collected two wins and two losses, bouncing back from defeat to level the score in both of his mini-matches . Anish Giri and Shakhriyar Mamedyarov stand 1 point behind the leaders.

Magnus Carlsen, rather surprisingly, stands fifth in Group C with 4 points, having drawn all four of his games. The Norwegian is the only player in the tournament yet to record either a win or a loss. What is more, he was fortunate to escape with a draw in his second encounter with Mishra, having reached a clearly inferior endgame. Despite his slow start, Carlsen remains only 2 points behind the leaders, while Mishra, in last place with 3 points, is also within striking distance. Note that only the group winners will have a chance to compete for tournament victory in the knockout stage.

Magnus Carlsen dealing with a tough endgame against 17-year-old Abhimanyu Mishra | Photo: Michal Walusza

Drawing twice against the best player in the world is a strong result - though Mishra later noted that "you should really win such a game" | Photo: Michal Walusza

The most notable result on Thursday was Bibisara Assaubayeva's victory with the black pieces over Arjun Erigaisi. Rated 2532, Assaubayeva defeated the 2746-rated Indian super-GM with the black pieces in their first encounter of the day ( see game with annotations below ), recording her first career win against a player rated above 2700.

Erigaisi bounced back to win their second game, but that does not take away from Assaubayeva's achievement. Following two draws against Wesley So on Wednesday, she has earned 11.4 rating points and climbed to fourth place in the women's live ratings .

Assaubayeva and Erigaisi share third place in Group D with 5 points each, 3 behind Niemann and Vachier-Lagrave. Wesley So, who first lost and then drew with Vachier-Lagrave on Thursday, stands fifth with 3 points. Reflecting on his results so far, the US representative remarked, "It's pretty clear I found my worst chess format".

It was a memorable day for Bibisara Assaubayeva, who managed to beat Arjun Erigaisi from the black side of a King's Indian Defence | Photo: Michal Walusza

Maxime Vachier-Lagrave is tied for first place in Group D, while Wesley So has failed to find his best form in Budapest | Photo: Michal Walusza

additionalSources.title: Caruana and Niemann score double wins on Day 2 in Budapest
additionalSources.summary: Thirteen decisive outcomes mark the second Fast Classic day as Assaubayeva defeats Erigaisi. Fabiano Caruana and Hans Moke Niemann each won both of their games on the second day of the Fast Classic group stage at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest, while Bibisara Assaubayeva recorded a standout victory over Arjun Erigaisi. Rounds 3 and 4 produced 13 decisive results from 24 games, three more than on the first day. Each player faced the same opponent twice with colours reversed. With three points awarded for a win and one for a draw, these two double victories earned Caruana and Niemann six points apiece. Alireza Firouzja now leads Group A outright on eight points, while Caruana heads Group B on ten. Ian Nepomniachtchi and Haik Martirosyan are level on six points at the top of Group C, and Niemann has joined Maxime Vachier-Lagrave on eight in Group D. Firouzja moves clear in Group A Alireza Firouzja played a long game with White and won over Jorden van Foreest and then drew the return encounter. The four-point haul takes him to eight overall, one point ahead of Jan-Krzysztof Duda. Duda and Nodirbek Abdusattorov exchanged wins with the black pieces. Duda prevailed in a long opening encounter, the longest game of the day, before Abdusattorov responded with victory in the return. Their three points apiece leave Duda on seven and Abdusattorov on four. Levon Aronian and Andrew Hong drew both games. Aronian moves to five points, with Hong on three. Van Foreest finishes the day on four. Caruana wins twice to take control of Group B Fabiano Caruana delivered one of the day’s strongest performances against Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu. With White, he sacrificed a piece to open the Black’s defences and won comfortably. He then added a with Black. The two victories put Caruana on ten points, two clear of Le Quang Liem. Liem Le remained his closest challenger after a win and a draw against Vincent Keymer. After winning a tough battle with White, Le finished the day on eight points, while Keymer has three. Richard Rapport and Vladislav Artemiev drew both encounters and move to three points each. Praggnanandhaa remains on two. Martirosyan joins Nepomniachtchi at the top as Carlsen draws twice Haik Martirosyan recovered from a first-game defeat against Anish Giri to win their return encounter. Giri’s attack brought him victory in as few as 26 moves with White, but Martirosyan stormed back in the return game. The three points lift Martirosyan to six, level with Ian Nepomniachtchi at the top of Group C, while Giri moves to five. Nepomniachtchi drew both games with Shakhriyar Mamedyarov. The pair added two points each, leaving Mamedyarov on five. Magnus Carlsen and Abhimanyu Mishra also drew twice. In the second game Mishra achieved a winning position but let his advantage slip away with one imprudent move in the opposite-colored bishops endgame. Carlsen has now drawn all four of his Fast Classic games and stands on four points, while Mishra has three. Niemann catches up with Vachier-Lagrave as Assaubayeva strikes Hans Moke Niemann collected the maximum six points against Vaishali Rameshbabu, winning both games. Niemann moved from two points to eight, while Vaishali remains on one. Maxime Vachier-Lagrave added four points to his tally in his match against Wesley So. He won the first encounter with White before drawing the return game, taking his total to eight and leaving So on three. Bibisara Assaubayeva scored one of the day’s most striking results by defeating Arjun Erigaisi with Black. Her advanced kingside pawns helped decide the first encounter, but Erigaisi responded with a Black win of his own. Both players finish the day on five points. The Fast Classic round-robin stage continues in Budapest on November 13, as the players compete for positions in the knockout brackets. Text: Total Chess Photos: Maria Emelianova and Michal Walusza Official website: www.totalchess.com About Total Chess Total Chess is a global championship platform established to redefine elite competitive chess for the modern era. Developed by Norway Chess and approved by FIDE, the Total Chess World Championship Tour introduces a unified format that crowns the world’s ultimate champion by testing excellence across three disciplines: Fast Classical, Rapid and Blitz. The Tour will bring together the world’s top 24 men and women players to compete across four premier international events hosted in leading global cities. Designed to elevate the sport’s commercial appeal and fan engagement, Total Chess combines world-class competition with innovation, technology and immersive spectator experiences to create a new benchmark for professional chess. With a vision to make chess one of the world’s most engaging and commercially sustainable sports, Total Chess aims to expand the game’s global footprint, inspire the next generation of players, and connect millions of fans through a dynamic championship that celebrates intelligence, strategy and sporting excellence.

title: Tony Miles: 25 years since the sudden death of an English star
summary:
Twenty-five years ago today, on 12 November 2001, English chess lost one of its finest players, Anthony Miles. He was the first English player ever to be awarded the title of international grandmaster by FIDE. Miles was among the world's top ten players for a time. His death came as a great surprise. | Photo: British Chess News

Anthony Miles, born on 23 April 1955 in a suburb of Birmingham, was already an outstanding chess talent at a young age. In 1968, he won the English Under-14 Championship and soon afterwards was already the strongest player in the English Midlands. In 1973, he finished runner-up in the World Junior Championship, and a year later he became world junior champion. In 1976, Miles became the first Englishman to receive the grandmaster title, and with it the £5,000 prize offered by the patron Jim Slater for achieving this feat.

During the 1970s and 1980s, Miles developed into a world-class player and attracted enormous attention when, at the 1980 European Team Championship in Skara, he defeated reigning world champion Anatoly Karpov with the highly unorthodox defence 1…a6. The move was not intended as a provocation. Miles had noticed that Karpov knew all his openings perfectly and wanted to lure the world champion out of his "comfort zone", as one would say today. It was not his only victory over Karpov.

This is a game everyone should know:

Miles was also a committed adherent of the Sicilian Dragon, which he regularly employed with success during the 1970s and 1980s.

In 1985, he played some of his games in Tilburg while lying on a stretcher because of back pain. The image went around the world.

Photo: Dutch National Archive

In 1986, Miles reached his highest position in the world top ten, rising to ninth in the rankings. Together with John Nunn, Nigel Short and Jonathan Speelman, he helped make the English national team one of the strongest in the world at the time. Only the Soviet team was stronger. Tony Miles' career, however, was repeatedly marked by setbacks for which he never found a satisfactory explanation.

Miles had a caustic sense of humour and never minced his words when he held a particular opinion. In 1987, he became involved in a dispute with Raymond Keene and the English Chess Federation over payments that Miles believed were unjustified. He also had a strained relationship with the rising Nigel Short. The continuing disputes affected Miles so badly that he suffered a nervous breakdown. Police detained him in Downing Street in September 1987, when Miles was apparently trying to reach Margaret Thatcher in order to speak to the Prime Minister about his dispute with the chess federation. Miles had to receive psychiatric care in a clinic for a period of time.

As a result of the disputes, Miles left the English federation and played for the US federation for a while. From 1988, he lived temporarily near Cologne in Germany.

Photo: British Chess News

In 1990, Miles won the US Championship. He also spent some time in Australia. In 1991, Miles returned to England and once again achieved good tournament results in the mid-1990s.

For ten years, Miles had also served as president of his chess club in Birmingham. The members knew him as a friendly, humorous and generous organiser. Miles also gave chess lessons and was not above teaching beginners, including children.

Miles v. Lawrence Trent at a tournament in Scarborough in 2001 | Photo: British Chess News

On 12 November 2001, an old school friend went to collect Miles to play bridge, but found him dead in his bed. Miles had died of heart failure, a consequence of long-term diabetes. His diabetes had almost certainly also been the cause of many of his episodes of weakness and periods of poor form. Remarkably, the illness had only been diagnosed three years before Miles' death.
